scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

The experience of fasting from dawn to sunset for an entire month can be transformative, and it's not uncommon for individuals to report changes in their perspective and values as a result. Research has shown that experiences like Ramadan can lead to increased empathy, self-awareness, and a greater appreciation for the struggles of others. The physical and emotional challenges of fasting can foster a sense of gratitude, humility, and compassion, which can, in turn, influence what people value most in life. Here are some possible ways that living through Ramadan might shape one's values: 1. **Appreciation for simplicity and gratitude**: The experience of fasting can help individuals appreciate the simple things in life, like food, water, and relationships. This can lead to a greater sense of gratitude and contentment. 2. **Empathy and compassion**: By experiencing hunger and thirst, individuals may develop a deeper understanding of the struggles of those who face food insecurity or other forms of hardship. This can foster empathy and a desire to help others. 3. **Prioritization of relationships**: The communal aspect of Ramadan, where families and friends come together to break their fasts, can strengthen social bonds and emphasize the importance of relationships. 4. **Spiritual growth and self-reflection**: The introspective nature of Ramadan can lead to a greater focus on one's spiritual growth, self-awareness, and personal development. 5. **Appreciation for the value of time**: The experience of fasting can help individuals appreciate the value of time and make the most of the time they have with loved ones. 6. **Resilience and self-discipline**: The physical and emotional challenges of fasting can build resilience and self-discipline, which can translate to other areas of life. 7. **Community and belonging**: The shared experience of Ramadan can create a sense of community and belonging, which can be a powerful source of motivation and support. It's essential to note that these changes in values and priorities can be highly individualized and may vary from person to person. Some people may experience a more profound shift in their values, while others may not notice significant changes. In your case, living through Ramadan every year can indeed shape your values and priorities. You may find that you appreciate the simple things in life more, develop a greater sense of empathy and compassion, or prioritize relationships and spiritual growth. The experience can also help you cultivate resilience and self-discipline, which can benefit you in many areas of life.
